headline: A Photonics Portfolio in Two Tiers: Rockets and Compounders
lede: The analyst known as Serenity divides his AI-optics slate into high-velocity bets and slow-burn compounders — a structure borrowed from private equity, applied to the fiber supply chain feeding AI data centers.
body:
The post reads like a shopping list, but the underlying logic is more deliberate than it looks. **Supply-chain chokepoint theory** — the idea that the most durable investment gains in a technology cycle accrue not to headline assemblers but to the narrow nodes they cannot substitute — runs through both tiers. Serenity, who built his audience mapping the photonics rotation before institutions arrived, has split his slate into companies with explosive near-term catalysts and ones he expects to compound quietly over years.

The "High Upside Rockets" share a common trait: each is either pre-revenue on its most important product or trading well below its addressable opportunity. *$SIVE* (Sivers Semiconductors, Nasdaq Stockholm) makes indium-phosphide laser dies — the active light source inside optical transceivers — at a moment when *co-packaged optics* (CPO, a design that embeds the optical engine directly into the switch chip to slash power and latency) is moving from lab prototype to hyperscaler deployment. Sivers shares ran more than 1,200% in the first four months of 2026, a rally that Swedish photonics analysts have publicly questioned as running ahead of fundamentals. *$AAOI* (Applied Optoelectronics) sits further along the maturity curve: 2025 revenue of $456 million already represents 83% year-over-year growth, and management is guiding past $1 billion in 2026 on an 800G and 1.6T transceiver ramp. **MSSCorp** (Taiwan Stock Exchange: 6830) is a Hsinchu-based semiconductor services firm covering materials analysis and optoelectronics supply chain work — relatively thinly covered outside Taiwanese markets. *PCL Technologies* (TWSE: 4977) manufactures optical transceiver modules and TO-Can packages, hitting an all-time high of TWD 257 in April 2026 and reporting a market capitalisation near TWD 17 billion.

The "Compounders" are a different species: large, established industrial groups whose optical divisions are a meaningful but not dominant share of total revenue, meaning the AI-buildout thesis is real but diluted. **Shunsin Technology** (TWSE: 6451), a Foxconn subsidiary, packages system-in-package (SiP) modules including fiber-optic transceivers and is accelerating its silicon-photonics and CPO deployment. The stock climbed roughly 263% over the prior year to around TWD 405 as of late April 2026. **Sumitomo Electric Industries** (Tokyo: 5802, ADR: SMTOY) is one of the largest global fiber-cable manufacturers; its fiber division benefits directly from hyperscaler spending on backbone and data-center interconnect cabling. Analysts at Goldman Sachs, Nomura, UBS, and Jefferies all carried buy ratings into spring 2026, with a consensus target near JPY 11,900 against a price near JPY 9,900. **Furukawa Electric** (Tokyo: 5801, ADR: FUWAY) in April 2025 spun its optical fiber operations into a joint venture called *Lightera*, which in March 2026 began mass production of 13,824-count cable — among the world's densest fiber count — for hyperscale data centers. *$COHR* (Coherent Corp.) and *$LITE* (Lumentum) are the most liquid names in the group, both recently added to the S&P 500. Coherent posted $5.8 billion in fiscal 2025 revenue (+23%) and announced availability of an industry-first dual-laser QSFP28-DCO module in March 2026; Lumentum's Q1 fiscal-2026 set a revenue record backed by an Nvidia strategic investment with multi-year purchase commitments.

What holds the two tiers together is the same underlying driver: the AI cluster build-out has created a structural demand surge for optical interconnect that copper cables cannot physically satisfy at the speeds and power budgets hyperscalers require. The debate among investors is essentially about timing and risk tolerance — whether the rockets have already priced in the next two years of execution, and whether the compounders' steadier growth will prove more durable than the valuation compression risk facing high-multiple pure-plays. Serenity's framing at least acknowledges both possibilities rather than collapsing them into a single narrative.

concepts.definition: A chip architecture that integrates optical transceivers directly alongside the switch or AI accelerator die in the same package, rather than connecting via pluggable modules and copper traces. CPO sharply reduces electrical signal loss and power consumption at very high data rates (800G and above), making it central to next-generation AI data-center design.

An investment framework that seeks narrow, hard-to-substitute nodes within a technology supply chain — components, materials, or processes that large downstream assemblers depend on but cannot easily source elsewhere. The theory holds that these chokepoints command pricing power and durable margins even when end-market competition is fierce.

A semiconductor compound used to fabricate high-speed lasers and photodetectors for fiber-optic communications. InP-based devices operate at the wavelengths favored in data-center interconnects (1310 nm and 1550 nm) and outperform silicon photonics on certain metrics including lasing efficiency, making InP substrate supply a bottleneck as optical transceiver volumes scale.

A combined transmitter-receiver module that converts electrical signals to light pulses for fiber-optic transmission and back again. Transceivers are labeled by their aggregate data rate (400G, 800G, 1.6T) and form factor (QSFP-DD, OSFP, etc.). They are the workhorse interconnect inside and between AI compute racks.

An assembly technique that integrates multiple chips, passive components, and sometimes optical elements into a single module. SiP packaging is used by companies like Shunsin to combine laser dies, drivers, and receivers into compact transceiver modules, reducing board space and improving signal integrity.
